text: The Master said, ‘I do not know how a man without truthfulness is to get on. How can a large carriage be made to go without the crossbar for yoking the oxen to, or a small carriage without the arrangement for attaching the horses?’
context_note: Truthfulness (xin) as the linchpin: without it a person simply cannot function in the web of relationships, as a carriage cannot move without its yoke-bar.

text: The Duke of She informed Confucius, saying, ‘Among us here there are those who may be styled upright in their conduct. If their father have stolen a sheep, they will bear witness to the fact.’ Confucius said, ‘Among us, in our part of the country, those who are upright are different from this. The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this.’
context_note: Confucius is contrasting mechanical truth-telling with the deeper integrity of sustaining family bonds; the passage is a locus classicus for the tension between honesty and relational duty, not a license for deceit.

text: The philosopher Yu said, ‘When agreements are made according to what is right, what is spoken can be made good.’
context_note: Promise-keeping is conditioned at the point of making: agreements accord with righteousness precisely so that keeping them will be possible and proper.

text: The great man does not think beforehand of his words that they may be sincere, nor of his actions that they may be resolute; — he simply speaks and does what is right.
context_note: Mencius subordinates literal fidelity to righteousness itself — the counterweight to rigid promise-keeping in the Confucian canon (Book IV, part B, ch. 11 in Legge's edition).

text: When you go abroad, behave to every one as if you were receiving a great guest; employ the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice; not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself; to have no murmuring against you in the country, and none in the family.
context_note: Ren described through hospitality's grammar: treat everyone as a great guest. The reciprocity rule follows in the same breath.

text: Tsze-kung asked, saying, ‘Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?’ The Master said, ‘Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.’
context_note: Shu — reciprocity — offered as the single life-rule; the negative golden rule that anchors Confucian other-regard.

text: There are men who say — ‘I am skilful at marshalling troops, I am skilful at conducting a battle!’ — They are great criminals.
context_note: Mencius's verdict on military prowess pursued as craft (Book VII, part B, ch. 4 in Legge's edition): the benevolent ruler has no need of such men; war-skill severed from righteousness is criminality.

text: The Master said, ‘To lead an uninstructed people to war, is to throw them away.’
context_note: War waged without long moral and practical preparation of the people is the ruler's betrayal of them — responsibility runs upward.

text: The Master said, ‘With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow; — I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud.’
context_note: Not wealth but wealth wrongly gotten is the floating cloud; the passage models contentment without renouncing prosperity as such.

text: The Master said, ‘Riches and honours are what men desire. If it cannot be obtained in the proper way, they should not be held. Poverty and meanness are what men dislike. If it cannot be avoided in the proper way, they should not be avoided.’
context_note: Desire for wealth is conceded as human; the proper way governs both getting and escaping. Acquisition is moralized at the means, not the end.

text: Chi K'ang, distressed about the number of thieves in the state, inquired of Confucius how to do away with them. Confucius said, ‘If you, sir, were not covetous, although you should reward them to do it, they would not steal.’
context_note: Theft is traced to the ruler's own covetousness: moral disorder flows downward, so the remedy for stealing begins with those who govern.

text: For a morning's anger to disregard one's own life, and involve that of his parents; — is not this a case of delusion?
context_note: From Fan Ch'ih's question about discovering delusions: a morning's rage endangering self and parents is the Analects' picture of anger as clouded judgment with relational cost.

text: The Master said, ‘The filial piety of now-a-days means the support of one's parents. But dogs and horses likewise are able to do something in the way of support; — without reverence, what is there to distinguish the one support from the other?’
context_note: Material support without reverence fails as filial piety: xiao is a disposition of the heart enacted in care, not a logistics problem solved.

text: The Master said, ‘In serving his parents, a son may remonstrate with them, but gently; when he sees that they do not incline to follow his advice, he shows an increased degree of reverence, but does not abandon his purpose; and should they punish him, he does not allow himself to murmur.’
context_note: Filial piety includes gentle remonstrance — obedience is not silence before parental error, but disagreement conducted inside reverence.

text: That male and female should dwell together, is the greatest of human relations.
context_note: Marriage as the greatest of the human relations (Book V, part A, ch. 2 in Legge's edition): the bond from which the five relations' web is woven, carrying duties of harmony and fidelity on both sides.

text: The Master said, ‘The superior man wishes to be slow in his speech and earnest in his conduct.’
context_note: Speech is disciplined toward action: the exemplary person underpromises and overperforms, and chatter about others has no place in that economy.

text: The Master said, ‘Fine words and an insinuating appearance are seldom associated with true virtue.’
context_note: Glibness as a moral warning sign: polished, ingratiating talk is the rhetorical form gossip and flattery share.

text: The Master said, ‘The superior man has a dignified ease without pride. The mean man has pride without a dignified ease.’
context_note: The distinction cuts between settled self-possession and its counterfeit: dignity needs no display, pride is display without substance.

text: Tsze-lu asked how a ruler should be served. The Master said, ‘Do not impose on him, and, moreover, withstand him to his face.’
context_note: Loyal service includes open opposition: the minister neither deceives nor flatters, but withstands the ruler to his face — remonstrance as duty, not betrayal.

text: To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage.
context_note: Courage is defined morally: the failure is not trembling before danger but seeing the right and leaving it undone.

text: The Master said, ‘The way of the superior man is threefold, but I am not equal to it. Virtuous, he is free from anxieties; wise, he is free from perplexities; bold, he is free from fear.’
context_note: Boldness free from fear stands with virtue and wisdom in the exemplary person's threefold way — courage as fruit of cultivation, not temperament.
